title: Tools for Substantive and Content Validity Pretesting
text: Hinkin-Tracey design, judge rates item every construct definition. rating_validity() treats dependence explicitly rather analyzing ratings independent groups. workflow combines two descriptive indices direct item-level screening: HTC (Hinkin-Tracey correspondence): strongly ratings match intended definition; HTD (Hinkin-Tracey distinctiveness): much intended-definition ratings exceed orbiting-definition ratings; one-way repeated-measures ANOVA item; planned paired contrasts comparing target definition orbiting definition. item-sort workflow, Retain Review screening labels rather automatic editorial decisions. output names strongest orbiting competitor weak item tells researcher conceptual overlap appears. Colquitt HTC/HTD labels applied target-scale averages, treated universal item-level cutoffs. Low-level components remain available:
code: set.seed(12) rating_dat <- expand.grid(   item = c("A1", "A2", "B1"),   rater = 1:20,   construct = c("A", "B", "C") ) rating_dat$target_construct <- ifelse(rating_dat$item == "B1", "B", "A") rating_dat$rating <- ifelse(   rating_dat$construct == rating_dat$target_construct,   pmin(5, pmax(1, round(rnorm(nrow(rating_dat), 4.4, .6)))),   pmin(5, pmax(1, round(rnorm(nrow(rating_dat), 2.1, .7)))) )  rfit <- rating_validity(rating_dat, scale_min = 1, scale_max = 5) rfit #> contentvalidR construct-rating analysis #> --------------------------------------- #> Items: 3 | Raters: 20 | Target scales: 2 | Constructs: 3  #> Design: within-judge ratings | Scale: 1 to 5  #> Item inference: one-way repeated-measures ANOVA (Greenhouse-Geisser corrected omnibus p) plus planned paired target-versus-orbiting contrasts  #> Planned-contrast adjustment: none  #> Judges: naive  #>  #> 3 item(s) meet the full item-level screening criterion; 0 item(s) are flagged for review. #>  #> Item-level evidence: #>  item target n_complete strongest_competitor  htc   htd p_value max_contrast_p #>    A1      A         20                    C 0.88 0.619       0              0 #>    A2      A         20                    B 0.84 0.531       0              0 #>    B1      B         20                    C 0.89 0.637       0              0 #>  recommendation #>          Retain #>          Retain #>          Retain #>  #> Target-scale Colquitt benchmark summary: #>  target n_items n_htc n_htd mean_htc htc_strength mean_htd htd_strength #>       A       2     2     2     0.86     Moderate    0.575  Very Strong #>       B       1     1     1     0.89       Strong    0.637  Very Strong #>  benchmark_set #>        overall #>        overall #>  #> Colquitt labels are empirical percentile norms for scale-level HTC/HTD averages, not universal cutoffs. #> HTC is an average rating and HTD is a difference between ratings, so they sit on #> different scales with different typical values. A high HTC can be labeled Weak in #> the same analysis where a much smaller HTD is labeled Very Strong. Compare each #> index against its own benchmark, never against the other index's number. #>  #> What these columns mean #>   htc -- Hinkin-Tracey Correspondence. Average rating of the item against #>       its intended construct definition, expressed as a proportion of the #>       rating scale. (0 to 1; higher is stronger) #>   htd -- Hinkin-Tracey Distinctiveness. How far the intended construct's #>       average rating exceeds the best competing construct's, as a #>       proportion of the rating scale. It is a difference, so its typical #>       values are far smaller than HTC's. (usually a small positive number; #>       higher is stronger) #>  #> What the status labels mean #>   Supported -- The evidence met the criteria set for this analysis. #>   Review -- Something here needs a closer look. Those words map #>   onto the shared statuses above. #>  #> See `contentvalid_glossary()` for all terms, or set  #> `options(contentvalidR.show_key = FALSE)` to hide this key. #>  #> 'Review' is not an automatic deletion decision.
